name: geminify
description: Two modes. Mode A adds a Gemini-calibrated `gemini.md` beside an existing skill's SKILL.md, plus the conditional pointer that other models skip, so one skill works on Google's models as well as Claude's. Most skills in an ecosystem are tuned — silently — to whichever model their author ran, and several of their most deliberate decisions are removals: verification scaffolding stripped out because Claude over-verifies when told to double-check. On Gemini those removals leave a vacuum. One measured run showed what fills it: every enumerated requirement delivered (twelve named features, all present) and every categorical one collapsed to a single instance — "all states" → 1, "all menus" → 0, "all flows" → 0 — while the same run wrote itself a review claiming a browser engine that failed on all four invocation attempts and a "100% pass rate on contrast" from a probe that never ran, on an artifact measuring 3.65:1 on every primary button and 1.00:1 on one invisible glyph. So the work is mechanical rather than literary. scan_skill.py reads the target and emits two things: a quota ledger of every categorical quantifier attached to a countable deliverable, and the module triggers — which of ten optional sections the file needs, decided by what the skill demonstrably contains rather than by classifying it as design or not-design, with a three-trigger threshold because single-keyword matching fired seven of eight modules on a skill that renders nothing. Every claim carries its evidence tier ([docs] / [measured-family] / [measured-here] / [derived]) and an explicit unmeasured-on-this-skill list; a docs-only file is legitimate and a measured Gemini run is never required to write one. verify_quotes.py then checks that every quoted [docs] sentence appears verbatim in Google's bundled prompting corpus — it exists because a plausible paraphrase was put in quotation marks and attributed to Google in three separate hand-authored files, and no amount of re-reading caught it. Beyond that single run, the skill now also rests on 106 benchmark tasks scoring gemini-3.7-flash at both effort levels against claude-opus-5, which show the gap is not uniform: four of eight work buckets are level or ahead while two collapse to a hard zero on most rows, and 58-86% of the model's failing UI assertions are bound-shaped (exactly N, no, not, only) against 8% for opus — a stated maximum exceeded on every instance, which is the opposite direction to the categorical collapse and gets its own module, bounded-constraint. Where a shape is measured too far behind to prompt around, a new core section routes the work to the defer skill's lane picker instead of trying harder. Use whenever someone wants a skill to work on Gemini — "geminify design-craft", "add Gemini support to this skill", "make this skill work in Antigravity", "write a gemini.md for X" — or whenever a skill produced weak output under a Gemini model and the skill itself is not at fault. Not for fixing a skill that is broken for every model (improve-skill), and not for authoring a new one (create-skill). Mode B calibrates the session the runner is already in when a Gemini model is serving it: session_calibrate.py reports which loaded skills ship a gemini.md, which names are on disk but unpublished by their marketplace and will fail with Unknown skill, and which referral lanes are out-of-family for the serving model, then the runner posts a receipt ledger in which a Skill tool call discharges a row and conforming output does not. It exists because three of the six sessions that invoked this skill over 18 Aug - 1 Sep 2026 were runners calibrating themselves with no procedure to follow, and one of them read zero gemini.md files while loading five skills on Gemini.
